clinicalPearls: Spermatic cord lipoma is the commonest benign tumour of the spermatic cord and paratesticular region and presents as a soft, painless inguinoscrotal swelling
Many so-called cord lipomas are extensions of retroperitoneal or preperitoneal fat drawn down alongside the cord rather than true encapsulated tumours
They are frequently discovered incidentally during inguinal hernia repair, where the fatty mass may be mistaken for or coexist with a hernia sac
On ultrasound the lesion shows fat-density echotexture and lies separate from a normal testis, helping distinguish it from an intratesticular tumour
The main differential of concern is a well-differentiated liposarcoma, which can appear similar but is larger, more heterogeneous, and may show thickened septa or non-fatty components
Symptomatic or enlarging lesions are treated by surgical excision, with histology to confirm a benign lipoma and exclude a liposarcoma
A large paratesticular fatty mass with atypical imaging features should raise suspicion of liposarcoma and prompt appropriate oncological assessment
reference.pathophysiology: A spermatic cord lipoma is a benign proliferation of mature adipose tissue within the cord, or an extension of preperitoneal or retroperitoneal fat that herniates down the inguinal canal alongside the cord structures. It grows slowly as a soft, well-defined fatty mass and, being extratesticular, does not involve the testicular parenchyma. Although benign, it must be distinguished histologically from a well-differentiated liposarcoma of the cord, which shares a fatty composition but carries malignant potential and a risk of local recurrence.
additionalDifferentials: Inguinal hernia containing omentum or bowel
Adenomatoid tumour of the paratesticular region
additionalInvestigations: Scrotal and inguinal ultrasound demonstrating a fat-density extratesticular mass with a normal testis
Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI) for larger lesions to characterise fat content and exclude liposarcoma
Clinical assessment for a coexisting inguinal hernia
Serum tumour markers when an intratesticular tumour cannot be excluded clinically
redFlags: A large or rapidly enlarging fatty mass suggesting liposarcoma
Heterogeneous imaging with thickened septa or non-fatty components
Associated symptoms such as pain or fixation to surrounding tissues
reference.prognosis: A true spermatic cord lipoma is benign and cured by excision with an excellent prognosis; the principal caveat is ensuring that a well-differentiated liposarcoma has not been overlooked, as the latter can recur locally and requires wider management.
pitfalls: Mistaking a well-differentiated liposarcoma for a simple lipoma
Assuming an inguinoscrotal fatty swelling is only a hernia and missing a cord lipoma or sarcoma
Failing to send excised tissue for histology
Confusing an extratesticular fatty mass with an intratesticular tumour
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Urinary and Male Genital Tumours
management: Surgical excision for symptomatic, enlarging or diagnostically uncertain lesions, with histology to confirm a benign lipoma
Excision or reduction of the fatty mass at the time of inguinal hernia repair when found incidentally
Histological exclusion of a well-differentiated liposarcoma, the main differential of concern
Cross-sectional imaging with CT or MRI for larger or heterogeneous lesions to assess fat content before surgery
Conservative observation with clinical follow-up for small, asymptomatic, clearly benign lesions
Refer to urology, and to a sarcoma service if liposarcoma is suspected
